doc.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Curved sopranos and Jan Garbarek's sound
summary: Both dislike curved sopranos, though Liebman admires Garbarek, whose stark declarative style fits his sound.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: But I think what you said about the Miles influence . . .

Definitely trumpet. It’s something about a straight horn. See, that’s the thing. There’s a difference between a thing that curves. Even the curved soprano I don’t like as much. There’s something about that versus that.
I hate curved sopranos. I think they should be lamps. I’ve rarely . . .
I think it’s a weird sound, although you hear yourself better. You do hear yourself better, because it’s coming up at you, but it sounds like – it sounds so squeaky to me.
Ugh. I don’t dig it. I don’t like the feeling of it either. I mean, if you’re going to be like this, let’s go. Let’s go. This? Who needs that? But . . .
Garbarek is the best curved soprano player ever.

Yeah, he’s great, and he has – because he has found his own sound. Also, he has a very bold, declaratory, emphatic way of playing, stylistically, that fits his tone. There’s nothing – it’s not Jimmy Giuffre. It’s not Chet Baker. There is nothing mysterious about it. That guy lays it down, like that, as coming from that part of the world, that’s the way they play. They’re very stark. It’s stark. It’s the way that landscape is up there, and that’s why it fits with him. But I’m not sure anybody else could get away with it, with the curve.
